title: Albert Cook's One-Year Trial: Opening Mengo Hospital in 1897
conflicts: Cook's arrival: 19 February 1897 (Foster, DACB) vs 15 February (hospital site; that was the lake party's date); story uses 19 February. First clinic: a shed already used as a dispensary (Foster, DACB) vs under a tree (hospital tradition); story follows the archival account. First ward: 15 May (Foster) vs 14 May (DACB) vs a June dedication (CMS report); story says mid-May. Patient numbers: CMS report 12,435 dispensary visits and 186 in-patients in nine months vs Foster's 17,000+ and 189 in the first year (and 141 in-patients for 1897); story uses only the CMS nine-month dispensary figure.
notes: Katharine Timpson was in the 1896 party and nursed at Mengo from 1897, but married Cook only in 1900, so she is credited as co-worker, not wife, in 1897. The slate's 'grass hut' is Foster's phrase; the story describes reed walls, thatch and a mud floor. Colonial context kept factual: protectorate, the doctor's first purpose being to care for missionaries, religious instruction as a condition of treatment, Mwanga's revolt; no judgement offered. Cook's own words come via Foster's quotations from his letters and the CMS report's extract of his journal; Uganda Memories (1945) and A Doctor and his Dog in Uganda (1903) are not online.
